newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin court curtails state cable regulation.
newsitem.headline: Berlin court curtails state cable regulation.

text.p: A Berlin court on Friday sided with Deutsche Telekom AG and prevented six private television stations from broadcasting over the company's cable system in the area of Germany's largest city.
Media authorities in Berlin and the state of Brandenburg did not have the right to allow stations to broadcast on the cable network without the permission of the network owner, the court ruled.
Telekom was reserving 15 channels on its cable system for digital programming that would be available in the future.

"The media authorities cannot make channels on the cable network available for broadcast use without the permission of Telekom because (the authorities) lack the legal basis to do so," a Berlin Justice Department summary of the ruling said.

The German government partially privatised Telekom last year, and the court said this measure meant that only the federal government -- and not the states -- could override decisions made by the cable provider.
As the network's owner, Telekom had the right to try to maximize profit and that restrictions by media authorities would have hindered its business strategy, the court said.
The media authority of Berlin and the MABB, its counterpart in Brandenburg, said they planned an appeal.
They had argued that because Telekom built the network as a public monopoly with public funds, the network should be subject to principles of media fairness as well as cartel law.
"It is more than strange to say that only market criteria apply here," an MABB spokeswoman said.
She added that the stations should be allowed to use the open cable slots as long as they were not needed for digital television.

The stations affected included the RTL network's Super RTL and children's channel Nickelodeon. Newspapers this week reported that the ProSieben Media AG planned to take over the German subsidiary of Nickelodeon.
